title: Authentic Kenyan Matoke
community: Luhya — widely enjoyed across Western Kenya and beyond
author: Mama Akinyi

regionalMap.alsoCommonIn: Nairobi, Kisumu, and all areas with large Western Kenyan communities

heritage.history: Matoke — unripe green bananas or plantains — has been a staple crop in Western Kenya for generations. In the Luhya community, banana plants are a defining feature of the agricultural landscape, grown in virtually every homestead. Cooking matoke in a tomato and onion sauce or simply steaming it has long been a central part of Luhya food culture, served at family meals, community gatherings, and celebrations alike.
traditionalUtensils: Banana leaves — for wrapping during steaming
heritage.modernEvolution: While the traditional method involves wrapping the green bananas in banana leaves and steaming them over a wood fire, modern Matoke is most commonly boiled and simmered in a tomato sauce on gas stoves. The dish has spread well beyond Western Kenya and is now enjoyed across the country.

desc: Kenyan Matoke is a deeply comforting dish of unripe green bananas or plantains simmered in a fragrant tomato, onion, garlic, and coriander sauce until completely tender and infused with flavour. The beloved staple of Western Kenya's Luhya community.
longDesc: Matoke is one of the great underrated staples of Kenyan cuisine. Unripe green bananas or plantains — firm, starchy, and almost potato-like in texture before they cook — transform completely during simmering, becoming soft, creamy, and deeply satisfying as they absorb the tomato sauce around them. In Western Kenya, no celebration meal is complete without a pot of matoke on the table.
ingredients: 8–10 green unripe bananas or plantains — peeled and halved

substitutions.alternative: Unripe plantains — both work equally well
Ground turmeric and cumin (half a tsp each)

steps: Peel the green bananas or plantains — green bananas can be tough to peel. Score along the ridges with a knife and remove the skin in sections. Halve or quarter to make even-sized pieces.
Place the peeled banana pieces in a bowl of cold salted water immediately after peeling to prevent browning.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the onions and cook until soft and lightly golden — about 6–8 minutes.
Add the garlic and ginger. Cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the diced tomatoes and tomato paste. Cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring, until completely broken down into a thick sauce.
Add the curry powder, salt, and black pepper. Stir for 30 seconds.
Drain the banana pieces and add them to the pot. Stir gently to coat with the tomato sauce.
Pour in the water or vegetable stock. Bring to a gentle boil.
Reduce heat to low, cover tightly, and simmer for 30–40 minutes until the bananas are completely tender when pierced with a knife.
Check and stir every 10 minutes, adding a little more water if the sauce is drying out.
When the bananas are fully tender and have absorbed the sauce, taste and adjust seasoning.
Scatter with fresh coriander and serve hot.
chefTips: Choose the firmest, most unripe green bananas available — any hint of yellow means the banana is starting to sweeten and will not hold its shape during cooking.
Soak the peeled pieces in cold salted water immediately — green bananas oxidise and brown very quickly once peeled.
Cook until completely tender — undercooked matoke is unpleasantly starchy and chewy.
For a richer dish, stir in a spoonful of peanut butter or coconut milk during the last 10 minutes.
commonMistakes: Using bananas that are too ripe — they become mushy and sweet during cooking.
Not soaking in water after peeling — the banana pieces turn black.
Undercooking — the starchy texture becomes unpleasant and hard to digest.
Too little liquid — the bottom scorches before the bananas are fully cooked.

faqs.q: What is the difference between matoke and regular bananas?
faqs.a: Matoke refers specifically to unripe, starchy green bananas or plantains used for cooking. They are completely different in flavour and texture from ripe sweet bananas — firm, starchy, and savoury rather than sweet.
No — ripe plantains become mushy and very sweet when cooked in a stew. For Matoke, always use firm, unripe green bananas or green plantains.

faqs.q: Is Matoke the same as Ugali?
faqs.a: No. Ugali is made from maize flour and has a smooth, dough-like consistency. Matoke is made from whole green bananas simmered in sauce and has a chunky, potato-like texture.
Yes — beef, goat, or chicken can be added. Brown the meat first, then follow the recipe from step 3. The meat simmers alongside the bananas and makes a heartier, complete meal.

cookingScience: Unripe green bananas are high in resistant starch — a type of starch that resists digestion in the small intestine and acts more like dietary fibre. As the bananas cook in liquid, the starch granules absorb water and gelatinise, softening the texture from firm and chalky to tender and creamy. This is why fully cooking matoke is essential — undercooked starch is difficult to digest and unpleasant in texture.
sustainabilityTips: Green bananas are available year-round and are among the most affordable and sustainable starch crops in East Africa.
Banana peels can be composted to enrich garden soil.
Buy from local Kenyan farmers’ markets when possible — supporting Western Kenyan agricultural communities.
storage: Refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 3 days. Not recommended for freezing as the texture changes significantly.
reheating: Reheat gently over medium-low heat with a splash of water, stirring occasionally until heated through.
healthBenefits: Rich in resistant starch — acts as a prebiotic, feeding healthy gut bacteria.
Good source of potassium and vitamin B6 — supports heart health and energy metabolism.
High in dietary fibre (8g per serving) — supports digestive health and long-lasting satiety.
Naturally low in fat and cholesterol-free.
Provides steady, slow-release energy from complex carbohydrates.
culturalNote: Matoke is one of the defining foods of the Luhya community in Western Kenya. Banana plants are a symbol of abundance and continuity in Luhya culture — planted in homesteads and harvested through the year. Serving matoke at a gathering is a gesture of warmth and generosity, and the dish remains central to celebrations, family meals, and community events throughout the region.
regionalVariations: Classic Luhya Matoke — simmered in tomato and onion sauce.
Matoke with beef — the most popular meat variation.
Matoke with groundnuts — peanut butter stirred in for richness.
Steamed Matoke — the traditional method wrapped in banana leaves.
Matoke with coconut milk — coastal-influenced variation.
Spicy Matoke — with extra chilli and pepper.
Matoke with fish — tilapia or omena added for a Western Kenya lake-region variation.
